gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the BLUETTI Apex 300's solar input window: two separate XT60 inputs, each 12–60 V and up to 20 A. That works out to at most 1,200 W per input (2,400 W total) without the SolarX 4K, so you can add panels to the kit's two 200 W panels only in strings under 60 V open-circuit voltage, one string per input. Going past 2,400 W of solar requires buying the separate SolarX 4K controller.
standout_why: I compared against StormWatts (cited; it has the most detailed solar-input table of the rival pages). It gives voltage windows for the Apex 200, Jackery HomePower 3000 (16–60 V, 12 A / 500 W per port, 1,000 W with both ports), EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra (11–60 V, 18 A, 800 W, one input) and others. For the Apex 300 it says only 'two native 1,200 W inputs' with 'voltage not stated', and it says nothing about MPPT. It does not cover the ALLPOWERS R3500 or BLUETTI Elite 300 at all. ChatGPT's own answers say only that 400 W of panels is 'relatively small' and give no voltage or current limits, so the shopper can't tell how far the included panels can be expanded. I did not reopen EnergySage, SolarGenAdvisor, Lights On Labs or Good Housekeeping. ChatGPT cited them only for prices and headline specs, not for input windows.
decides: This supports the Apex 300 kits as the expandable-solar option for shoppers who can wait (dispatch late January 2027 per today's table). Each of its two inputs has its own MPPT tracker and accepts 12–60 V and up to 20 A, so the two included 200 W panels can each take one input, and more panels can be added up to about 1,200 W per input without extra hardware. It does not change the ships-now pick, which in our range is an ALLPOWERS R3500 kit (+ SP037 400 W at a $1,586.73 link price, or + SP039 600 W at $1,753.93). I could not source the R3500's own input window from a page I opened, so the page should not claim a solar-mechanism advantage either way for the R3500.
